pos: n. (proper name; a daughter of Pharaoh who married into Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Bithyah, daughter of the LORD, from bath (daughter) and the divine element -yah. For an Egyptian princess to bear such a name is itself a testimony.
biblical_def: Bithiah is named once: “And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). A Pharaoh's daughter married a man of Judah, and her children are enrolled in the tribe of the promise. The name is the striking thing. Bithyah means daughter of the LORD, compounded with the covenant name, and an Egyptian princess did not receive such a name at birth in the house of Pharaoh. The likeliest reading — and the dictionary offers it as a reading, not a certainty — is that this was a name taken, as Ruth took the God of Israel and Rahab took her place in Jericho's wall on the side of the LORD. If so, the Chronicler has quietly recorded a conversion. The genealogy of Judah, which runs toward David and toward Christ, contains a Gentile woman out of the house that had enslaved Israel, and it names her daughter of the LORD. “And Esrom begat Aram” is how the line reads in Matthew; but the line has Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba in it, and in Chronicles it has this woman too.

corruption_summary: Israel's genealogies are read as records of ethnic purity; they repeatedly enrol Gentiles who joined themselves to the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The common charge is that Old Testament Israel was defined by blood and closed to outsiders. The genealogies themselves are the refutation. Judah's line holds Tamar, Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabitess, and here a daughter of Pharaoh bearing a name compounded with the covenant name of God. Scripture does not hide these women; Matthew names three of them in the first chapter of the New Testament.

The principle to recover is that the covenant was always entered by faith and not by descent. “Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the LORD, speak, saying, The LORD hath utterly separated me from his people” (Isaiah 56:3). What Ezra later opposed was not foreign blood but foreign gods, and Bithiah is the case that proves the distinction: a foreign woman named daughter of the LORD, married into Judah, with her sons in the record.

pos: n. (proper name; a daughter of Solomon, wife of Ahimaaz)
etymology: Hebrew Basemath, spice or fragrance, from a word for balsam and sweet spices. The form is close to Bashemath, the name of one of Esau's wives, but the women are distinct and centuries apart.
biblical_def: Basmath is named once: “Ahimaaz was in Naphtali; he also took Basmath the daughter of Solomon to wife” (1 Kings 4:15). She is a daughter of Solomon, married to one of his twelve officers over the districts of Israel, each of whom provided victuals for the king's household a month in the year. Her sister Taphath had married another of them, the son of Abinadab over the region of Dor (1 Kings 4:11). So two of Solomon's daughters were given to two of his regional officers — dynastic marriages binding the administration to the throne. She is to be distinguished from Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, one of Esau's wives some seven centuries earlier; the spelling is near, the women are not the same. Her name means fragrance, and the dictionary cannot resist noting where her father's wisdom literature ends up on that subject: “Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart” (Proverbs 27:9), and, less happily for Solomon, “Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour: so doth a little folly him that is in reputation for wisdom” (Ecclesiastes 10:1).

corruption_summary: Similar spellings are merged into one person; Solomon's daughter and Esau's wife are distinct women centuries apart.
corruption_paragraphs: Basmath of 1 Kings 4:15 and Bashemath of Genesis 26:34 are near enough in spelling to be confused, and the dictionary keeps them apart because Scripture does: one is a daughter of Solomon given to an officer of his kingdom, the other a Hittite woman who married Esau some seven centuries earlier. Near-identical names in a long history are ordinary; collapsing them produces a phantom person.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is care in handling the record. The one-entity rule of this dictionary cuts both ways: one person must not be given two entries, and two persons must not be crushed into one. Scripture names people precisely, and reading it well means honouring the distinctions it draws as well as the ones it refuses.

pos: n. (proper name; second wife of Jerahmeel and mother of Onam)
etymology: Hebrew 'Atarah, a crown — the ordinary Hebrew word for a crown or wreath, used of royal diadems and of garlands.
biblical_def: Atarah is named once: “Jerahmeel had also another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam” (1 Chronicles 2:26). That single sentence is the whole of her record, and the clause the Chronicler chose to attach is she was the mother of Onam. Her name means a crown, and the dictionary will not pass that by, because Scripture itself makes the connection between crowns and the quiet honour of a household. “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” (Proverbs 12:4), and the mother of the man speaking in Proverbs 31 is remembered for teaching him. Atarah's line continues: Onam's sons are named in the verses that follow, and his house is tracked through the genealogy of Judah. She is in the Bible because she bore a son, and a woman named crown whose recorded glory is motherhood is exactly the pattern the dictionary holds up, against an age that treats the bearing and raising of children as an interruption of a life rather than a great part of its honour.

corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of the age is that bearing and raising children subtracts from a woman's significance, so that a record which remembers a woman as a mother has diminished her. Scripture holds the reverse. A woman named crown is remembered in the genealogy of the tribe of promise for the son she bore, and the Bible's longest passage in praise of a woman ends with her children rising up to call her blessed.

The principle to recover is that children are an heritage of the LORD and the fruit of the womb His reward (Psalm 127:3). The dictionary holds the creational order of Genesis 1 and 2 and the complementarian pattern of Ephesians 5 and 1 Peter 3, in which the honour given to wife and mother is real honour and not a consolation. Atarah is one line in a long chapter, and the line is a crown.

pos: n. (proper name; a wife of Shaharaim the Benjamite)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'ara, of uncertain meaning; a connection with a root meaning to burn or to kindle has been proposed, as has a reading the brutish, neither with certainty.
biblical_def: Baara is named once, in a verse of unusual sadness: “And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives” (1 Chronicles 8:8). The clause after he had sent them away is doing something, and the Chronicler does not explain it. The plainest reading is that Shaharaim put away these two wives and afterward had children by another in Moab; the verses following name the sons of Hodesh, a third wife. The dictionary declines to build a story the text does not give, and records what the text gives: a Benjamite in a foreign country, two wives sent away, a household broken and the pieces written down. There is no commendation anywhere in the passage. Scripture is willing to put such a verse in a genealogy without comment, which is part of its honesty; it does not present the covenant people as a gallery of sound marriages. What God says about the practice He says elsewhere and plainly: “Let not the husband put away his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:11). Baara is a name attached to a grief, and the Bible keeps it.

corruption_paragraphs: The present age regards the ending of a marriage as a personal matter with no party to answer to, and the churches have largely followed. Malachi 2:16 is the verse that cannot be accommodated to that view: the LORD saith that He hateth putting away, and names it dealing treacherously, and warns the man to take heed to his spirit. The Chronicler gives no comment on Shaharaim; the prophets supply it.

The principle to recover is the permanence of the marriage covenant. “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6). The dictionary holds marriage as one man and one woman covenanting before God for life, and holds also that Scripture's honesty about broken households — recorded without approval, in a bare genealogical clause — is part of how it teaches.

pos: n. (proper name; a wife of David and mother of Ithream)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eglah, a heifer — the ordinary Hebrew word for a young cow, used of the red heifer and of the heifer of the broken neck.
biblical_def: Eglah is named twice, each time in the list of sons born to David at Hebron: “And the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron” (2 Samuel 3:5), and “the sixth, Ithream by Eglah his wife” (1 Chronicles 3:3). She is the sixth and last named, and she is the only one of the six whom the text calls David's wife in so many words — the others are named simply as the mothers. Nothing else is told of her, and her son Ithream is never heard of again. The dictionary marks the setting, because the Hebron list is the beginning of a long sorrow. Six wives in Hebron and more in Jerusalem; and out of that house came Amnon's crime, Absalom's revenge and revolt, Adonijah's grasping, and Tamar's ruin. The law had said of a king, “Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away” (Deuteronomy 17:17), and David multiplied wives, and his heart and his household paid. Eglah is a name in the list that is the quiet beginning of the house's grief.

corruption_summary: David's polygamy is treated as divinely sanctioned because it is narrated; the law forbade it and the narrative shows the cost.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Scripture records David's many wives without an explicit rebuke at the point of listing them, it is often said that the Bible endorses polygamy. It does not. The law governing kings had already forbidden multiplying wives, and the books of Samuel then narrate, at length and in detail, the ruin that came out of that house — incest, fratricide, rebellion, and a dying king's contested succession.

The principle to recover is that Scripture frequently teaches by consequence rather than by commentary, and that its standard for marriage is Genesis 2:24 as Christ cited it: one man, one woman, one flesh. The dictionary holds that standard and reads the Hebron list as the law's warning being ignored by the best king Israel had.

pos: n. (proper name; wife of Aaron and mother of the priestly line)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elisheba', God is an oath or God of the oath, from 'el (God) and sheba' (oath, seven). It is the Hebrew name behind the Greek Elisabeth.
biblical_def: Elisheba is named once, and the verse carries the whole Aaronic priesthood: “And Aaron took him Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Naashon, to wife; and she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar” (Exodus 6:23). Every legitimate priest in Israel for the next fifteen centuries descended from this woman's sons. Two of the four died young: Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire before the LORD, which He commanded them not, and were consumed (Leviticus 10:1; Numbers 3:4). The priesthood therefore ran through Eleazar and Ithamar, and so to Zadok and to Abiathar, and so to Zacharias in the temple — whose wife, Luke records, was of the daughters of Aaron and named Elisabeth, which is this same name. The dictionary marks that quiet symmetry: the mother of the priesthood and the mother of its last herald bore one name, God is an oath. The oath is the point. “The LORD hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Psalm 110:4) — and Hebrews reasons from that oath to a better priesthood than Aaron's.

corruption_summary: The strange-fire judgment is read as disproportionate; Scripture names the offence as worship God commanded not.
corruption_paragraphs: The death of Nadab and Abihu is among the passages most often cited as evidence of an arbitrary God. The text states the offence with precision: they offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not. The sin was not carelessness with a flame but innovation in worship by men ordained to conduct it, on the day the priesthood began.

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship, which this dictionary holds: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add. Two of Elisheba's four sons died establishing that rule, and the priesthood that continued through the other two was conducted by men who had watched it happen.

pos: n. (proper name; father of the prophet Hosea, and a Hittite father-in-law of Esau)
etymology: Hebrew Be'eri, my well or man of the well, from be'er (a well) — the word behind Beersheba and Beer-lahai-roi.
biblical_def: The name belongs to two men. The first is a Hittite whose daughter Esau married: “And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite” (Genesis 26:34) — a marriage that, with his second, was a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah. The second is the father of a prophet: “The word of the LORD that came unto Hosea, the son of Beeri” (Hosea 1:1). That is all Scripture tells us of Hosea's father, and it is the standard formula: the prophetic books open by naming a man and his father and the kings of his day, grounding the word of the LORD in a particular household at a particular time. The dictionary notes how much weight that formula carries. Prophecy in Israel was not anonymous oracle; it came to named men with fathers and dates, and Hosea's word was tested against the reigns of four kings of Judah and one of Israel. And the word that came to this man was the hardest commission given to any prophet: to marry a wife of whoredoms and so to preach, with his own household, God's covenant love for an adulterous people.

corruption_paragraphs: Much modern handling of the prophets detaches the oracles from the men, assigning the material to schools, redactors and layers. The books themselves resist it in their first verses. Hosea is the son of Beeri and spoke in the days of four named kings of Judah and one of Israel; the claim is historical and falsifiable, and the dictionary takes it as given rather than as a literary frame.

The principle to recover is that revelation came to real men in datable reigns, which is why it can be believed. Hosea's commission went further: his own marriage was made a sermon, so that the word was not only spoken by a man but suffered by him. “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms” (Hosea 1:2) is not a literary device; it is what God told the son of Beeri to do.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Hadad, an early king of Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Bedad, commonly read alone or solitary, from a root meaning to be separate or by oneself.
biblical_def: Bedad is named twice, both times only as a father: “And Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who smote Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Avith” (Genesis 36:35), repeated at 1 Chronicles 1:46. He belongs to the list of kings who reigned in Edom, and that list carries a sentence worth stopping over: “And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel” (Genesis 36:31). Esau's line had kings while Jacob's line had none. Edom was organised, settled and crowned generations before Israel came out of Egypt, and from any worldly vantage the wrong brother was prospering. Scripture records the fact without anxiety, because the promise was never that the elect line would be first or grandest. It was that the promise ran through Jacob. “As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated” (Romans 9:13). Bedad's son wore a crown while Israel was in brick-kilns, and the covenant was with the brickmakers.

corruption_summary: Worldly precedence is read as divine favour; Edom had kings for generations while the covenant line had none.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct to read prosperity as approval is as old as Asaph's envy of the wicked, and Genesis 36 sets up the test plainly: Esau's line produced a succession of kings before Israel had one. By every visible measure the rejected brother was ahead, and Scripture states it in a single unembarrassed verse.

The principle to recover is that election is not read off outcomes. “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated” (Romans 9:13) is Paul's summary, and he draws it from exactly this history. Edom's crowns were real and came first; the promise was elsewhere. A Christian measuring God's favour by his circumstances is making Edom's mistake in reverse.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Elihu the Buzite in the book of Job)
etymology: Hebrew Barakh'el, God hath blessed, from barakh (to bless) and 'el (God).
biblical_def: Barachel is named twice, both times in the identification of his son: “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God” (Job 32:2), and again at Job 32:6, where Elihu begins to speak. His son is the fourth speaker and the hinge of the book. Elihu had waited while three older men argued with Job and failed, and when he spoke he said why he had waited and why he would wait no longer: “I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” (Job 32:6), and then, “But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding” (Job 32:8). Notice the ground of his correction: not Job's suffering but Job's self-justification — because he justified himself rather than God. That is the fault the whirlwind addresses in the chapters following, and Elihu is the only one of the four friends God does not rebuke at the end. The son of a man named God hath blessed is the one who insisted that God be justified rather than man.

He is named only as the father of Elihu the Buzite.

scriptures: Job 32:2
Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God.
Job 32:6
And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion.
Job 32:8
But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
Job 40:8
Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?
corruption_summary: Job's complaint is read as wholly vindicated; Elihu names the actual fault, that Job justified himself rather than God.
corruption_paragraphs: Job is widely read as a book that endorses the sufferer's protest without qualification, since God does rebuke the three friends at the close. But the narrator himself tells us what Elihu was angry about, and it is not Job's pain: because he justified himself rather than God (Job 32:2). The whirlwind then presses the same charge — wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?

The principle to recover is that the sufferer's grief is honoured while his self-justification is not. God vindicates Job against the false comfort of Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, and still requires Job to abhor himself and repent in dust and ashes. The dictionary holds both, as the book does, against a reading that makes the afflicted man the measure of God's righteousness.

pos: n. (proper name; a Reubenite, father of Bela)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azaz, strong or he is strong, from a root meaning to be strong or mighty — the root behind Uzziah, Uzzi and Aziza.
biblical_def: Azaz is named once, in a Reubenite genealogy: “And Bela the son of Azaz, the son of Shema, the son of Joel, who dwelt in Aroer, even unto Nebo and Baalmeon” (1 Chronicles 5:8). The verse locates his son's household in the high pastureland east of Jordan, and the chapter that holds it ends badly. A few verses later the Chronicler records that these eastern tribes — Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh — “transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land” (1 Chronicles 5:25), and that God stirred up the Assyrian kings, who carried them away first of all Israel. Azaz's name means strong. The tribes he belonged to were strong: the same chapter says they were valiant men, that they made war on the Hagarites and prevailed, and that they prevailed because “they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them, because they put their trust in him” (1 Chronicles 5:20). The strength was real and borrowed; and when they stopped crying, it went. They were the first tribes into exile and the first to have had the point explained to them.

He was a Reubenite, the father of Bela, who dwelt at Aroer.

scriptures: And Bela the son of Azaz, the son of Shema, the son of Joel, who dwelt in Aroer, even unto Nebo and Baalmeon:

And they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him.
And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them.

And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day.
corruption_summary: Victory is credited to the strength of the victors; the Chronicler credits it to their crying out, and names what followed when they stopped.
corruption_paragraphs: Military success invites the conclusion that strong men make their own outcomes, and the eastern tribes had every ground for it: valiant men, skilled in war, who beat the Hagarites and took enormous spoil. The Chronicler names the real cause in the same sentence — they cried to God in the battle, and He was intreated of them, because they put their trust in Him.

The principle to recover is that strength held without dependence does not last. Seventeen verses after the victory the same tribes are whoring after the gods of the land, and the God of Israel stirs up Assyria against them. They were the first carried away. A man named strong stands in the genealogy of the tribes that learned where their strength had been coming from by losing it.
